question: Which is NOT one of the five purposes of topdressing shown in the module's star diagram?
correct: relieving soil compaction
feedback: The five: controlling thatch, smoothing surface, protecting greens in winter, changing the growth medium, promoting recovery.

question: The practice of topdressing originated to:
correct: keep golf and bowling greens smooth
options: keep golf and bowling greens smooth
control thatch buildup on golf fairways
feedback: Smoothing came first; other benefits were observed later.

question: Before specialized equipment, topdressing was applied with:
correct: hand shovels
feedback: Manual application with shovels.

question: Non-uniform hand application of topdressing can result in:
correct: differential wilting or localized dry spots
options: differential wilting or localized dry spots
marcelling and scalping of the green
severe soil compaction beneath the coring holes
grain and stolon buildup on the green
feedback: Plugs show the contrast between well and inadequately topdressed turf.

question: Specialized topdressing equipment is used mainly to ensure:
correct: uniform application
feedback: Uneven application caused dry spots.

question: Traditional topdressing preparation involves screening and blending loam or sandy loam soil, medium-to-coarse sand, and:
correct: peat moss or other organic materials
options: peat moss or other organic materials
crushed gravel or other coarse materials
feedback: Three constituents screened and blended.

question: The sand component of a traditional topdressing blend is:
correct: medium-to-coarse sand
feedback: Blended with loam/sandy loam and peat moss.

question: Sand topdressing has become increasingly popular because of:
correct: increased traffic stress and higher quality standards
options: increased traffic stress and higher quality standards
lower sand prices and much easier application methods today
reduced thatch production in modern cultivars
the shortage of loam soils near golf courses
feedback: An alternative to blended soil topdressing.

question: When topdressing immediately follows core cultivation, the remaining medium not in the holes may:
correct: fill thatch pores or form a layer above the thatch
options: fill thatch pores or form a layer above the thatch
wash completely out of the turf with irrigation
compact the soil at the very base of the coring holes
be collected and reused at the next application
feedback: Part fills the holes; the rest goes into or onto the thatch.

question: Properly filling aerification channels with topdressing leads to:
correct: quicker recovery of the turf
feedback: The filled holes stay visible until covered by adjacent growth.

question: The portion of topdressing that fills cultivation holes remains clearly evident until:
correct: covered by growth of adjacent turfgrass plants
options: covered by growth of adjacent turfgrass plants
the next core cultivation removes it again
it is washed out of the holes by heavy rain or irrigation
the green is matted with a heavy steel mat
feedback: Most other topdressing is obscured by shoots and thatch.

question: In the turf-soil profile, the sand "finger" resulted from:
correct: filling a cultivation hole with sand
options: filling a cultivation hole with sand
a crack in the soil from drought
a root channel left by old grass
an earthworm burrow filled with sand
feedback: Successive topdressings dramatically change the growth medium.

question: The thin soil layer above the lowermost sand layer in the profile probably resulted from:
correct: reincorporating cores after sand topdressing began
options: reincorporating cores after sand topdressing began
topdressing with soil before the green was built
a single heavy rain washing silt into the green
vertical mowing that pulled native soil up from far below
feedback: Reincorporated cores after starting a sand program.

question: Once a sand topdressing program begins, soil cores from hollow-tine cultivation should be:
correct: removed from the site before topdressing
options: removed from the site before topdressing
reincorporated with a steel mat right away
left on the surface to break down naturally
mixed with the sand and spread back out
feedback: Otherwise texturally different layers form.

question: Texturally different layers from mixing sand topdressing with reincorporated soil cores interfere with:
correct: root growth and water and air movement
options: root growth and water and air movement
mowing quality and the ball-roll distance on the green
seed germination on the surface only
feedback: Layers seriously interfere with root growth and water and air movement.

question: Besides reincorporating soil cores, layering can also occur where sand is:
correct: not effectively incorporated into the thatch
options: not effectively incorporated into the thatch
applied at a light rate every week
matted in with brushes or smooth rakes
used to fill the holes left behind after core cultivation
feedback: Sand sitting atop thatch forms its own layer.

question: The rate and number of topdressing applications are limited by:
correct: the capacity of the turf to absorb the material
options: the capacity of the turf to absorb the material
the size and capacity of the topdressing equipment used
the cost of sand in the local market
the number of core cultivations per year
feedback: Too much prevents light from reaching leaves.

question: Excessive amounts of topdressing can lead to substantial turf loss by:
correct: preventing light from reaching the leaves
options: preventing light from reaching the leaves
raising the soil pH beyond optimal levels
introducing weed seeds into the green
compacting the soil beneath the thatch
feedback: Light exclusion.

question: Which topdressing purposes require LARGE amounts of material?
correct: smoothing big irregularities and changing root-zone soil
options: smoothing big irregularities and changing root-zone soil
protecting greens in winter and promoting recovery
light thatch control and promoting the recovery from disease
marking spray areas and overseeding the green
feedback: Both need frequent applications of considerable quantities.

question: Per the module's photo caption, the factor that may be most important in setting topdressing amount is:
correct: turfgrass growth
feedback: The amount depends on several factors, though growth may be most important.

question: For thatch control, the AMOUNT of topdressing sand depends on:
correct: the amount of thatch present
feedback: Amount ↔ thatch present; frequency ↔ accumulation rate.

question: For thatch control, the FREQUENCY of topdressing depends on:
correct: the rate thatch is accumulating
options: the green speed wanted for upcoming tournament play
feedback: Amount ↔ thatch present; frequency ↔ accumulation rate.

question: If topdressing rates and frequencies are too low:
correct: excessive organic residue persists in the profile
options: excessive organic residue persists in the profile
the thatchlike derivative becomes too firm to play
the green loses all of its resiliency over time
sand layers form on top of the compressed thatch
feedback: Too little sand leaves too much thatch.

question: If too much sand is applied, the thatchlike derivative may lack:
correct: resiliency and ball-holding capacity
feedback: Too much sand makes the surface too hard.

question: Per the thatch-sand proportion diagram, more thatch relative to sand gives:
correct: higher resiliency, but possibly too spongy
options: higher resiliency, but possibly too spongy
lower resiliency, and a harder surface
higher resiliency, and better ball roll
feedback: Thatch bounces back but may be spongy.

question: Topdressed turfs are usually matted with:
correct: a heavy steel mat
feedback: Matting works the sand or soil into the turf.

question: Compared with a heavy steel mat, brushes for working in topdressing cause:
correct: considerably less wear damage
feedback: An alternative to steel mats.

question: Which method of working in topdressing causes the LEAST damage to turf?
correct: smooth rakes
feedback: Even less damage than brushes.

question: With sand topdressing on dense thatch, instead of migrating into the thatch pores, the sand may:
correct: form a distinct layer atop the thatch
options: form a distinct layer atop the thatch
dissolve into the organic matter quickly
wash down through the thatch completely
bind with the thatch into a single crust
feedback: Especially in dense thatch such as a Penn A-4 green.

question: Sand is especially likely to form a layer atop the thatch where the thatch is:
correct: relatively dense, as in Penn A-4 greens
options: relatively dense, as in Penn A-4 greens
relatively thin, as in new USGA greens
relatively loose, as in Kentucky bluegrass
relatively dry, as in dormant bermudagrass
feedback: Dense thatch resists sand infiltration.

question: The weight of a sand layer atop thatch:
correct: compresses the thatch and reduces its porosity
options: compresses the thatch and reduces its porosity
loosens the thatch and increases its overall porosity
has no effect on the thatch beneath it
speeds decomposition of the thatch layer
feedback: The thatch becomes fine-textured relative to sand.

question: Relative to the topdressing sand, compressed thatch is a:
correct: finer-textured medium
feedback: Compression reduces porosity.

question: Successive sand topdressings over dense thatch can create alternating layers of:
correct: coarse sand and fine compressed thatch
options: coarse sand and fine compressed thatch
fine sand and coarse loose thatch
coarse gravel and fine native soil
fine silt and coarse organic matter
feedback: A texturally layered profile.

question: Alternating layers of sand and compressed thatch impede:
correct: infiltration into and percolation through the green
options: infiltration into and percolation through the green
root growth only in the topmost sand layer
green speed only, with no effect on water movement through it
feedback: Texturally distinct layers impede water movement.

question: Layering from sand and compressed thatch can be avoided by:
correct: a more frequent sand topdressing program
options: a more frequent sand topdressing program
a less frequent but heavier sand program
switching to soil instead of sand
rolling the green after each topdressing
feedback: Frequent light applications prevent distinct layers.

question: On a Penn A-4 green, topdressing should be conducted:
correct: weekly
feedback: Dense thatch requires frequent topdressing.

question: Where sand and thatch layers have already formed, bypass drainage channels can be created by:
correct: coring followed by heavy sand topdressing
options: coring followed by heavy sand topdressing
rolling followed by light sand topdressing
feedback: The sand-filled holes pass through the layers.

question: An alternative to coring for existing layers is shallow vertical mowing to:
correct: remove some thatch and open up the rest
options: remove some thatch and open up the rest
compact the thatch for a firmer surface
bury the sand layer beneath the thatch
sever stolons and reduce grain on greens
feedback: Facilitates subsequent sand incorporation.

question: In newly planted turfs, rolling is performed to:
correct: firm the bed for good plant-soil contact
options: firm the bed for good plant-soil contact
smooth out frost heaving in spring
press divots back into the soil
feedback: Contact between planting material and soil.

question: In established turfs, rolling corrects minor surface disruptions and:
correct: reestablishes soil contact with turf torn by play
options: reestablishes soil contact with turf torn by play
removes thatch accumulated at the surface
increases water infiltration into the compacted surface soil
feedback: Sections loosened or torn by play.

question: Large, heavy rollers were commonly used in the Northeastern US to:
correct: smooth fairways in spring
feedback: A traditional practice later recognized as compacting.

question: Many traditional rolling practices were abandoned because of:
correct: the severe soil compaction of heavy rolling
options: the severe soil compaction of heavy rolling
the high cost of buying and running large rolling equipment
damage to irrigation pipes from rolling
the scalping caused by heavy rollers
feedback: Recognized as turfgrass technology progressed.

question: Lightweight rolling of greens has enjoyed a resurgence since the:
feedback: Part of superintendents' success in maintaining fast putting speeds.

question: The success of many superintendents in maintaining fast putting speeds is attributable, in part, to:
correct: a rolling program
feedback: Lightweight rolling increases green speed.

question: Rolling can be done with a triplex greens mower by:
correct: replacing the reel units with rollers
options: replacing the reel units with rollers
raising the reels above the turf
removing the bedknives from the reels
adding ballast to the mower frame
feedback: Interchangeable units.

question: Rolling has enjoyed a resurgence on greens since the 1990s with:
correct: relatively lightweight units
feedback: Heavy rolling was abandoned once its compacting effects were recognized.
source: Textbook Ch. 6, pp. 201-207: Rolling, Topdressing, and Matting

question: Rolling after planting ensures:
correct: contact between soil and planting materials
options: contact between soil and planting materials
faster germination of weed seed in the soil
deeper penetration of the irrigation water
removal of excess thatch from the surface
feedback: Seed, stolons, sprigs, plugs, and sod.
source: Textbook Ch. 6, pp. 201-207: Rolling, Topdressing, and Matting

question: In climates with freezing winters, rolling is used to:
correct: press heaved turfgrasses back into the soil
options: press heaved turfgrasses back into the soil
break up the thick ice layers that cover the turf in winter
remove snow mold from the leaf surface
firm the soil before snow cover arrives
feedback: Otherwise heaved plants may desiccate or be scalped.
source: Textbook Ch. 6, pp. 201-207: Rolling, Topdressing, and Matting

question: At the time of rolling, the soil should be:
correct: moist but not wet
feedback: Dry soil resists pressing; wet soil compacts.
source: Textbook Ch. 6, pp. 201-207: Rolling, Topdressing, and Matting

question: Sod growers often roll before harvest to:
correct: ensure uniform sod thickness
feedback: Allows shallower cuts and lighter sod.
source: Textbook Ch. 6, pp. 201-207: Rolling, Topdressing, and Matting

question: Rolling of greens is regarded as an alternative to:
correct: ultra-low mowing heights for fast speeds
options: ultra-low mowing heights for fast speeds
core cultivation for relieving soil compaction
feedback: Especially on sand-based greens that resist compaction.
source: Textbook Ch. 6, pp. 201-207: Rolling, Topdressing, and Matting

question: The three basic types of rollers are drum rollers, triplex-attachment rollers, and:
correct: dedicated greens rollers
feedback: Greens rollers were introduced in the early 1990s.
source: Textbook Ch. 6, pp. 201-207: Rolling, Topdressing, and Matting

question: An advantage of triplex-attachment rollers is that:
correct: no extra operator training is needed
options: no extra operator training is needed
they are the heaviest rollers made
they do not compact soil at all
they double as vertical mowers for grain control
feedback: They are operated like a triplex mowing unit.
source: Textbook Ch. 6, pp. 201-207: Rolling, Topdressing, and Matting

question: Nikolai et al. (2001) found that lightweight rolling once or twice per week:
correct: raised green speed for 24-48 hours
feedback: Rolling four or more times per week could raise bulk density and reduce infiltration and quality.
source: Textbook Ch. 6, pp. 201-207: Rolling, Topdressing, and Matting

question: Rolling four or more times per week could result in:
correct: higher bulk density and lower infiltration
options: higher bulk density and lower infiltration
lower bulk density and higher infiltration
no change in any soil property at all
faster green speed lasting a full week
feedback: One or two rollings per week caused no significant change.
source: Textbook Ch. 6, pp. 201-207: Rolling, Topdressing, and Matting

question: Ancillary benefits of rolling that have spurred fairway rolling include reduced:
correct: dollar spot, moss, and black cutworms
options: dollar spot, moss, and black cutworms
brown patch, algae, and white grub damage
snow mold, clover, and mole crickets
feedback: Bird activity associated with cutworms also declined.
source: Textbook Ch. 6, pp. 201-207: Rolling, Topdressing, and Matting

question: Topdressing is believed to have originated specifically to:
correct: smooth the playing surface of greens
options: smooth the playing surface of greens
feedback: Thatch reduction was observed later as a side effect.
source: Textbook Ch. 6, pp. 201-207: Rolling, Topdressing, and Matting

question: Where a submerged layer of sand exists within a soil profile, the soil above it is often:
correct: persistently wet, with restricted rooting
options: droughty, with very deep rooting into the subsoil
compacted, with no change in moisture
feedback: Even small differences among layers have significant adverse effects.
source: Textbook Ch. 6, pp. 201-207: Rolling, Topdressing, and Matting

question: When starting a sand topdressing program, core reincorporation should wait until the sand depth exceeds:
correct: the cultivator's maximum penetration depth
options: the depth of the thatch layer above the soil
one inch below the putting surface
the mowing height of the green
feedback: Otherwise alternating sand and soil layers form.
source: Textbook Ch. 6, pp. 201-207: Rolling, Topdressing, and Matting

question: Where the indigenous soil is favorable, the topdressing soil should be:
correct: identical to it
feedback: Stockpile extra soil when building a new green.
source: Textbook Ch. 6, pp. 201-207: Rolling, Topdressing, and Matting

question: The only difference between a construction soil and a topdressing soil is the amount of:
correct: organic amendment
feedback: The turf generates enough organic residue on its own.
source: Textbook Ch. 6, pp. 201-207: Rolling, Topdressing, and Matting

question: Which is NOT a listed concern over sand topdressing?
correct: a softer playing surface
feedback: Sand layers give a HARDER playing surface.
source: Textbook Ch. 6, pp. 201-207: Rolling, Topdressing, and Matting

question: A rule of thumb is to topdress for thatch control when the thatch layer becomes:
correct: "pencil thick" (about 0.25 inch)
feedback: Then apply about 0.2 yd³/1000 ft², a layer about 0.0625 inch.
source: Textbook Ch. 6, pp. 201-207: Rolling, Topdressing, and Matting

question: In the integrated topdressing soil-thatch medium, the thatch provides:
correct: resiliency and aeration
feedback: The soil provides firmness and water/nutrient retention.
source: Textbook Ch. 6, pp. 201-207: Rolling, Topdressing, and Matting

question: Per O'Brien and Hartwiger (2003), light, moderate, and heavy sand topdressing rates are:
feedback: USGA Green Section rates.
source: Textbook Ch. 6, pp. 201-207: Rolling, Topdressing, and Matting

question: For bentgrass/annual bluegrass greens, light topdressing rates should be used in:
correct: summer
feedback: Slow growth means slow organic matter accumulation; for bermudagrass, light rates go in spring and fall.
source: Textbook Ch. 6, pp. 201-207: Rolling, Topdressing, and Matting

question: For bermudagrass greens, moderate topdressing rates are used in:
correct: summer
feedback: When growth and organic matter accumulation are most rapid.
source: Textbook Ch. 6, pp. 201-207: Rolling, Topdressing, and Matting

question: Total seasonal sand for topdressing plus filling HTC holes should be at least:
feedback: About 4000-5000 lb/1000 ft², or a 0.5-0.6 inch depth.
source: Textbook Ch. 6, pp. 201-207: Rolling, Topdressing, and Matting

question: Dust and particulate matter in sand topdressing can be managed by periodically:
correct: coring and filling holes with clean sand
options: coring and filling holes with clean sand
rolling the green with a heavy drum roller
applying wetting agents every few weeks
raising the mowing height for a season
feedback: Or by topdressing often enough to dilute the particulates.
source: Textbook Ch. 6, pp. 201-207: Rolling, Topdressing, and Matting

question: Years of topdressing can raise the level of a USGA green, making its surface:
correct: droughty
feedback: Compensate by coring and core removal.
source: Textbook Ch. 6, pp. 201-207: Rolling, Topdressing, and Matting

question: Matting is usually necessary after topdressing to:
correct: work soil off foliage and into the turf
options: work soil off foliage and into the turf
remove thatch along with the excess topdressing soil
firm the surface for faster speeds
feedback: Adhering soil would interfere with mowing and putting.
source: Textbook Ch. 6, pp. 201-207: Rolling, Topdressing, and Matting

question: When soil cores are too wet for matting, the soil tends to:
correct: smear
feedback: Too dry, and the cores are hard and bricklike.
source: Textbook Ch. 6, pp. 201-207: Rolling, Topdressing, and Matting

question: Before modern herbicides, matting was used to:
correct: lift decumbent crabgrass shoots for mowing
options: lift decumbent crabgrass shoots for mowing
bury weed seed below germination depth
spread herbicidal salts over the turf
pull broadleaf weeds out by the roots
feedback: Uplifted shoots could be mowed more easily.
source: Textbook Ch. 6, pp. 201-207: Rolling, Topdressing, and Matting

question: Matting after vertical mowing serves to "ribbon" debris, which:
correct: facilitates removal of the debris
options: buries the debris into the thatch
grinds the debris into fine dust
feedback: Seed can be left in place while debris is removed.
source: Textbook Ch. 6, pp. 201-207: Rolling, Topdressing, and Matting
